subject: Lily-Rose-Depp
research_tasks: After Werwulf opens (US Dec 25, 2026; UK Jan 1, 2027), collect her press interviews and run the settle test in the discriminator: when she describes what steadied her through playing a grounded medieval mother, does she credit trusted people, Eggers's structure and preparation (6) or her own distinct feeling and identity (4)? Update C08, C106 and C107 tense and dates.
Eggers's "disciplined, courageous, and, like, feral" line (Complex, S21) is not used in the draft; if an editor adds it, find its original interview first or attribute it as quoted by Complex.
The draft attributes the Idol production claims through Rolling Stone's May 23, 2023 follow-up (S12) and ET (S11). If an editor quotes the March 1, 2023 report directly, open the original first.

The draft quotes ELLE France (March 26, 2026) only as reported by Purepeople (S37), with the author's translations; open the original interview if accessible before adding more of it. Vogue Australia (S36) is not quoted in the body.

The draft mentions only that Amber Heard made an allegation in a Los Angeles court in May 2016 (CBS/AP, S14) and that a 2022 defamation trial took place (S41). It describes no allegation, evidence or verdict; keep it that way unless reliable reporting on each proceeding is opened and every claim attributed.

sources.title: "I'm a Sucker for a Crazy Love Story": Lily-Rose Depp, by Natalie Portman (Interview Magazine, Winter 2024/25 cover)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp in conversation with Natalie Portman (call dated Oct. 25, 2024)
sources.locator: Full Q&A transcript; passages on prep and choreography (early), fear and daredevilry (middle), the "backpack" answer, anchoring people, and dual cultures (late)
sources.excerpt: "Prep is so interesting because you never know if you're doing it right." / "I was grateful not to have to shape it on my own." / "I used to be way more daredevil-ish when I was a kid, and now I'm scared of everything." / "I think the world started to scare me a lot. I'm super scared of things that I used to not be scared of. It's weird." / "I wonder if I'm more aware of the dangers of the world or something? But I would never jump out of a plane." / "Everything is mental. I'm good. I'm chilling." / "You have all your super-private feelings in your backpack, and you go to work and the scene starts and you let it out." / "you have to have people around you that you've known forever that are going to anchor you." / "I feel like I've always been full of dualities, and my double culture adds to that." / "No, I am so scared." / "This industry can be so crazy and you can lose your footing really easily. I feel like it's corny because people always say this, but you have to have people around you that you've known forever that are going to anchor you." / "I love going to the butcher and the grocery store and having dinner at my friends' houses." / "That's when things get dangerous, when you don't see those things as valuable anymore." / "I've grown up being taught that your private life and your inner life is so precious, and that it really needs to be protected."
sources.context: Long phone conversation with a friend she met at 16 (Portman cast her in Planetarium). The fear lines come in a laughing exchange about going to space, skydiving, bungee jumping and zip lining, then she contrasts herself with people who say "So fun, what a rush." The backpack line follows "I've grown up being taught that your private life and your inner life is so precious, and that it really needs to be protected." The dualities line is about being called "so American" by French friends and "French girl" by American friends; she adds "my family's French, so when I'm with them, I feel like I'm 100 percent French, and when I'm with my dad's side of the family, I'm like, yeah, we're all Kentuckians." Portman names her partner [070 Shake]; Depp later refers to "a lazy morning with my boyfriend." Promotional interview for Nosferatu, conducted by a friend.

sources.title: Lily-Rose Depp on The Idol and growing up famous (i-D, The Timeless Issue no. 371, Spring 2023)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp, interviewed by Alex Frank
sources.locator: Cover story; paragraphs on Abel Tesfaye ("Talk about trust and comfort"), Tusk and Chanel origins, her mother's photos, imposter syndrome, paranoia about photos, and the nepo-baby discussion
sources.excerpt: "Talk about trust and comfort. I had to go to a lot of really vulnerable places in the show. Abel was the best partner that I could have ever asked for. He has my back and I have his," / "You just have to jump in and have some kind of faith that, if they've chosen me, then hopefully I've been chosen for a reason. That's all that you can do," / "If you're not scared, then what's the point? I like the fear a little bit." / "I overthink, like, 'If I leave my house and I look like shit and someone takes a photo, is it going to be, 'She looks like hell, she must be depressed?'" / "I bring myself back down to earth and go, 'Girl, you don't matter that much.'" / "I'm so careful about these conversations now." / "You're so much prettier than me." She's so beautiful." / "Okay, I really don't want to fuck this up, so let me work as hard as I possibly can to make sure that I have left no rock unturned." / "If I leave my house and I look like shit and someone takes a photo, is it going to be, 'She looks like hell, she must be depressed?'"
sources.context: Zoom cover interview before The Idol aired. The writer calls her "charming and sweet, if endearingly jittery," and frames the imposter-syndrome passage himself ("Like many sensitive souls, Lily-Rose is plagued by imposter syndrome"). The "chosen for a reason" line is followed by "Wow, I'm so nervous... You could ask for no better fuel to make you want to work really, really hard" and "let me work as hard as I possibly can to make sure that I have left no rock unturned." The mother comparison is described as said "lovingly" and "half-joking." The piece also states that her first role came on the set of Tusk, a film her father was in, where she was "pretty casually told to jump into a scene," and that Chanel is a house "her mum had worked with since the 90s."

sources.title: What's It Like Being Lily-Rose Depp? Keira Knightley Finds Out (Interview Magazine, September 2021 issue)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp in conversation with Keira Knightley
sources.locator: Full Q&A transcript; answers on role choice ("weird and wonderful"), on-set anxiety, leaving school at 16, and being judged through her parents
sources.excerpt: "Weird and wonderful is definitely the direction I'm trying to go." / "It's possible for me to get in my head and be like, 'Am I going to be able to do this? What have I signed up for? Are they sure that I'm the one?' Random things like that. But I always try to remind myself that if anything, it's a sign that I'm invested and excited and wanting to do the best job possible." / "And trust is so huge. There's so much to be said about feeling comfortable and connected with your partners, with your director, and with your crew members." / "I have really strong gut instincts" / "Of course. Those fears are—not fears, but those thoughts are totally normal." / "I'm not the same kind of actor as my dad or my mom, and I'm very much my own person."
sources.context: Conversation with her Silent Night co-star. The anxiety answer responds to Knightley's direct question, "Do you ever suffer from anxiety on set or stage fright?" Her first move is self-talk (nerves mean she is invested; "I would also be worried if I didn't have that feeling"), then trust in partners, director and crew, then the hair and makeup trailer as "such a sacred place." The "my own person" answer responds to "Were you worried, because of who your mom and dad are, that you'd be judged differently?" and ends "that doesn't mean you can't become your own artist, or that your own art isn't valuable on its own." She also says she left school at 16 because "I'm unable to not immerse myself in something completely when I'm doing it."

sources.title: Lily-Rose Depp Is An Idol Rising (ELLE US, December 2022/January 2023 cover)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp, interviewed by Véronique Hyland
sources.locator: Cover story; passages on privacy and her father ("secret garden"), strangers and anxiety, nepo baby, the audition, Levinson and Tesfaye, and the show's provocativeness
sources.excerpt: "When it's something that's so private and so personal that all of a sudden becomes not so personal…I feel really entitled to my secret garden of thoughts. I also think that I'm not here to answer for anybody" / "But I've just been raised in a manner that has taught me that privacy is something that's important to protect." / "I'm not here to give myself to the world to be eaten alive." / "that they're going to think I'm really weird or rude because I just get really shy and kind of anxious," / "At the end of the day, what really matters to me is what my family and friends and loved ones think of me." / "Maybe you get your foot in the door, but you still just have your foot in the door." / "I did not think at all that this was going to go my way," / "two people who make me feel incredibly safe and protected," / "I'm not interested in making anything puritanical. I'm not interested in making anything that doesn't challenge me, or challenge other people, honestly," / "That's why I like to do my work and put as much of my heart into it as I can and then retreat back into my real life and just be a normal person." / "I know my childhood didn't look like everybody's childhood" / "nothing is going to get you the part except for being right for the part"
sources.context: Interview at her mother's Los Angeles home during The Idol shoot, published while her father's 2022 trial was recent. The writer describes a "self-effacing woman" who apologized for lateness and stressed punctuality, and calls her "Ever careful." In the same piece she says "I know my childhood didn't look like everybody's childhood" (before the nepo-baby backlash) and "my parents protected my brother [Jack] and me from it as much as possible." Of expecting to lose The Idol she adds "I know that everybody and their mother goes in for these things." The safety line continues "I think it's difficult to do this kind of work that can be so vulnerable in so many different ways if you don't have a lot of trust between you and your collaborators." She also says "There's nothing more fun to me than sinking my teeth into something," and the writer says the scrutiny "doesn't intimidate her."

sources.title: Lily-Rose Depp's Road to Nosferatu: "People Have Been Ready to See Me Fail" (Vanity Fair, Awards Insider)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp, interviewed by David Canfield
sources.locator: Intro paragraphs and full Q&A; answers on the Zoom audition, butoh, one-take scenes, method acting and "the darkness home," big emotional roles, The Idol, insecurity, and "ready to see me fail"
sources.excerpt: "I was really nervous," / "I wanted to show that I wasn't scared to go there." / "I thought for sure it wasn't going to go my way." / "It's an emotional outlet for me—I feel like it helps me, I don't know, heal things with myself, perhaps. I feel like a lot of us do this for that reason." / "Nobody wants to be the one that messes it up for everybody, which brings this real team feeling. I felt a lot of support from everyone, especially in those scenes that were more demanding." / "I don't intend on being method because I wouldn't know how to—I'm too attached to my life, I feel like." / "This movie had such an immersive energy about it that I do think I brought the darkness home, for sure." / "I also just feel like I'm better at crying than laughing, which—I don't know what that says about me as a person. [Laughs] I laugh a lot in my own life. I'm a happy person, so I like to explore the underbelly of that at work." / "But I stand by it. We made a choice and we went for it." / "I'm very close with Sam and Ashley [Levinson]. They're like family to me." / "Getting over the imposter syndrome of, like, 'Why am I here and why do these people think that I can do this?'" Getting to a place where I felt confident enough within myself to be like, "I can do this and I am here for a reason," I definitely have struggled with that. Humility is incredibly important, especially in this business." / "I feel like people have been ready to see me fail, in a way, since I was a kid. That has made me only want to work harder and prove people wrong." / "trying to find my own identity in this world" / "If people still want to talk shit or see me in a certain way, then that's not my problem. I've had to grow into that feeling as well." / "One of the sides was a big freak-out scene, and I made sure that I had a bunch of stuff to throw. I had a roll of paper towels, and some books, and I just threw shit all over the room. I started moving around like crazy. I wanted to show that I wasn't scared to go there." / "I really like emotional scenes because they're challenging. I feel stimulated by that." / "I'm not on Twitter. I'm not reading stuff." / "I like to do things that maybe not everybody's down to do." / "looking like a corpse every day. [Laughs] It was a workout for my self-esteem." / "Yeah, but it just is what it is."
sources.context: Awards-campaign interview at a Beverly Hills cafe. The insecurity answer responds to "Have you struggled with insecurity in this business?" and continues "I definitely was walking in being like, 'Oh my God, I am so out of my depth.' But you just have to be like, 'You know what? I may feel this way, but I have to go to work tomorrow.'" The "darkness home" paragraph directly follows the method-acting answer and continues "I was carrying her with me when I was at home." The "team feeling" line is about one-take scenes involving "the dolly grip, and the focus puller, and the cameraman." The big-roles answer responds to "you definitely gravitate toward bigger, emotional characters" and also says "I gravitate more toward bigger, emotional performances because I like the challenge of it." On The Idol she adds "I loved the experience of making it—that was a huge turning point for me." The writer says Eggers "needed someone uninhibited and fearless" and that she "has consistently felt insecure about making her own way as an actor."

sources.title: Rare Bloom: Lily-Rose Depp combines star power with commitment to her craft (Harper's Bazaar UK, February 2025 issue)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp, interviewed by Sasha Slater
sources.locator: Profile from a November 2024 lunch in London; passages on Edward Scissorhands, gothic instincts, dualities, loyalty, 070 Shake, and the 2024 US election
sources.excerpt: "I was traumatised by it," she recalls. "Not because I thought he was scary, but because everyone was being so mean to him and I got really upset." / "It's a difficult childhood memory. Edward's the good guy and Nosferatu's kind of the bad guy, but there's a part of me that feels a little bit of empathy for Nosferatu. I mean, am I sick for feeling that way?" / "I'm interested in the darker underbelly of things," / "The most exciting thing is getting to explore parts of myself. You get to hide behind all these beautiful artifices, the costumes, the story, but the place I'm drawing from is deeply personal." / "There are so many sides to me," she says. "I really feel that paradox in myself." / "I love people who love their people," / "I've always been really private about my personal life, but it's hard not to talk about her because I'm so happy." / "It's a horrific time, and I'm scared, and I'm sad." / "When things feel out of control and you feel powerless, you have to hold tight to the people you love and look after those people." / "We're very different actors, but of course you're the product of your environment"
sources.context: Promotional profile for Nosferatu. The writer frames loyalty ("Loyalty... ranks highly for Depp"); her words are "I love people who love their people... When you find people who feel real and you connect with them, you have to hold onto that." The election lines follow "I feel we're going backwards, which is endlessly disheartening and heartbreaking." The writer reports that for two years she has been with Danielle Balbuena (070 Shake), whom Depp calls "'my boyfriend', because that's what she feels like." She also says "I don't think I'm a shy person necessarily... But I'm shy when people come up to me" and "nothing is straightforwardly dark, it's the most complicated stuff."

sources.title: 'The Idol': The Weeknd, Lily-Rose Depp, HBO Defend Series After Report Says It's 'Disgustingly Off the Rails' (Entertainment Tonight)
sources.speaker: Lily-Rose Depp (statement to ET); HBO statement; reporter Zach Seemayer
sources.locator: Article body; HBO statement and Depp's full statement
sources.excerpt: "Sam is, for so many reasons, the best director I have ever worked with. Never have I felt more supported or respected in a creative space, my input and opinions more valued. Working with Sam is a true collaboration in every way - it matters to him, more than anything, not only what his actors think about the work, but how we feel performing it. He hires people whose work he esteems and has always created an environment in which I felt seen, heard, and appreciated."
sources.context: Issued the day after Rolling Stone's March 1, 2023 report on the show's production. Her statement describes her own experience as the lead. HBO's statement in the same article: "The initial approach on the show and production of the early episodes, unfortunately, did not meet HBO standards so we chose to make a change," and the team was "committed to creating a safe, collaborative, and mutually respectful working environment."

sources.title: 'The Idol' Team Responds to Rolling Stone Expose: 'They Can Write Whatever They Want' (Rolling Stone)
sources.speaker: Jon Blistein (Rolling Stone), quoting Lily-Rose Depp and Sam Levinson at the Cannes press conference
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs 2-4 and 7
sources.excerpt: Interviews with 13 members of the show's cast and crew revealed claims that the show's on-set working conditions were often chaotic and that the series had taken a dark turn. / "I just wanna say that it's always sad and disheartening to hear mean, false things about someone you care about, and it wasn't my experience shooting the show." / Levinson's scripts reportedly contained disturbing sexual and physically violent scenes between Depp and Tesfaye's characters, three sources told Rolling Stone. / In fact, Rolling Stone did include statements from Depp, HBO, and a source close to the production, all of whom defended the series and on-set environment. / "When I read the specifics, however, it just felt completely foreign to me."

claims.claim: Lily-Rose Melody Depp was born on May 27, 1999, in Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, to actor Johnny Depp and singer-actress Vanessa Paradis. She grew up between Los Angeles and France with her younger brother, Jack.
claims.passage: She was born on May 27, 1999, in Neuilly-sur-Seine, outside Paris, to the actor Johnny Depp and the French singer and actor Vanessa Paradis, and grew up between Los Angeles and France with her younger brother, Jack

claims.claim: She left school at 16 to act, explaining to Keira Knightley (2021): "I have really strong gut instincts, and I felt like, 'You know what? This is my moment to transition into the next phase of my life.'" She was already working at the time.
claims.passage: She left school at 16 on her own call. "I have really strong gut instincts," she told Knightley.
claims.inference: Self-report; the school decision is an early, self-directed choice made on instinct.
claims.alternative: Leaving school was possible because she was already working and had family resources; it shows decisiveness, which an anxious-type reading must account for.

claims.claim: Her first screen role came at 14 on the set of Kevin Smith's Tusk (2014), a film her father was in, where she was "pretty casually told to jump into a scene" (i-D, 2023). Smith's daughter Harley Quinn Smith was her childhood best friend; at 16 she said her parents agreed because "My parents trust Kevin a lot."
claims.passage: Her first role came at 14, on the set of Kevin Smith's _Tusk_, a film her father was in, where she was "pretty casually told to jump into a scene,"
claims.inference: Establishes the family connection behind her first role, which is part of the context for later nepo-baby criticism.

claims.passage: French and independent films followed, including _The Dancer_ (2016), which earned her a César nomination, and _The King_ (2019).

claims.claim: In 2021, asked by Keira Knightley whether she suffers from anxiety on set, she said "Definitely," that it peaks right before she starts something, with thoughts like "Am I going to be able to do this? What have I signed up for? Are they sure that I'm the one?" Her answer then reframes the nerves ("it's a sign that I'm invested and excited") and names trust: "And trust is so huge. There's so much to be said about feeling comfortable and connected with your partners, with your director, and with your crew members."
claims.passage: Her first move in that answer is her own self-talk. The nerves are "a sign that I'm invested and excited and wanting to do the best job possible." Her second move is other people: "And trust is so huge. There's so much to be said about feeling comfortable and connected with your partners, with your director, and with your crew members."
claims.inference: Two steadying moves in one answer: self-talk that normalizes the anxiety, then trust in collaborators. The doubt is about capability and about whether the people who chose her were right.
claims.alternative: A direct question from a co-star invites a confession of nerves; the self-talk half is an inward resolution, so this source does not show an outward-only pattern.

claims.claim: In February 2023 she said of imposter feelings: "You just have to jump in and have some kind of faith that, if they've chosen me, then hopefully I've been chosen for a reason. That's all that you can do," and that nerves are "fuel": "let me work as hard as I possibly can to make sure that I have left no rock unturned." She added, "If you're not scared, then what's the point? I like the fear a little bit."
claims.passage: "You just have to jump in and have some kind of faith that, if they've chosen me, then hopefully I've been chosen for a reason. That's all that you can do."
claims.inference: Here doubt is answered by faith in the judgment of the people who chose her, plus exhaustive preparation, and fear is kept and used as energy.
claims.alternative: The surrounding paragraph is framed by the writer; the "chosen for a reason" line is a single statement. Converting nerves to effort also fits Types 3 and 1.

claims.claim: In November 2024 she called the hardest part of Nosferatu "getting over the imposter syndrome of, like, 'Why am I here and why do these people think that I can do this?'" and continued: "Getting to a place where I felt confident enough within myself to be like, 'I can do this and I am here for a reason,' I definitely have struggled with that. Humility is incredibly important, especially in this business." On set she felt "so out of my depth" but told herself, "I may feel this way, but I have to go to work tomorrow."
claims.passage: "Getting to a place where I felt confident enough within myself to be like, 'I can do this and I am here for a reason,' I definitely have struggled with that. Humility is incredibly important, especially in this business."
claims.inference: The hoped-for resolution here is inward ("within myself") and dutiful, and she says reaching it has been a struggle. This qualifies the outward-steadiness reading: inner confidence is the goal, but she describes it as hard to reach.
claims.alternative: Counterevidence to a purely outward pattern. "Humility is incredibly important, especially in this business" names a professional norm, so volunteered doubt could also be image management (Type 3) for an actor labeled a nepo baby.

claims.claim: Of the Nosferatu Zoom audition she told Vanity Fair (November 2024), "I was really nervous," and, early in the interview, "I thought for sure it wasn't going to go my way." She said the same of The Idol in 2022 ("I did not think at all that this was going to go my way"), and her mother said in 2023 she had done many castings where she was not chosen. On the January 2025 podcast she said she is usually relaxed about auditions but "I really, really want this one."
claims.passage: "I was really nervous," she said of that audition, and she had assumed she would lose: "I thought for sure it wasn't going to go my way."
claims.inference: Anticipation of a negative outcome on the roles she wanted most, alongside a borrowed belief that tempers ordinary auditions.
claims.alternative: Realism about competitive auditions; the "chill" account cuts against a picture of constant audition anxiety, and accepting fate can read as Type 9.

claims.claim: In February 2023 she told i-D, directly after her self-talk about not wanting to mess up, "If you're not scared, then what's the point? I like the fear a little bit." Of the Nosferatu audition: "I wanted to show that I wasn't scared to go there" (2024). Of people wanting her to fail: "fuel to my fire" (2024).
claims.passage: Then, in the next breath: "If you're not scared, then what's the point? I like the fear a little bit."
claims.inference: Fear is named and converted into energy for work, which matches the 9takes triad framing of the Six as the type that uses fear.
claims.alternative: She also frames the same choices as appetite and taste: "I really like emotional scenes because they're challenging. I feel stimulated by that" (2024); "There's nothing more fun to me than sinking my teeth into something" (2022). The roles demanded extremity (Eggers "needed someone uninhibited and fearless"), so meeting the brief is not proof of a fear motive.

claims.claim: Asked by Natalie Portman (October 2024 call) about the most daredevil thing she had done, she said, "I used to be way more daredevil-ish when I was a kid, and now I'm scared of everything."
claims.passage: "I used to be way more daredevil-ish when I was a kid, and now I'm scared of everything."
claims.inference: Fear about her own life outside the work; with C52-C57 it is the hard emotion she most often names about herself (count in C36).
claims.alternative: A laughing exchange about space travel, skydiving, bungee jumping and zip lining, as the article says; it should not be read as a stated lasting state. In 2021 she corrected herself, "Those fears are—not fears, but those thoughts are totally normal."

claims.claim: She repeatedly names trust and safety as the condition for vulnerable work: of Levinson and Tesfaye, "two people who make me feel incredibly safe and protected... I think it's difficult to do this kind of work that can be so vulnerable in so many different ways if you don't have a lot of trust between you and your collaborators" (Elle, 2022); also "Talk about trust and comfort" (i-D, 2023), "I've never felt more respected and more safe on a set, honestly" (Vogue Australia via ET, 2023) and "trust is so huge" (2021).
claims.passage: in 2022, are "two people who make me feel incredibly safe and protected."
claims.inference: Safety and trust in specific people are her stated precondition for risk, repeated across 2021-2025.
claims.alternative: This is standard language for sexually explicit or physically demanding productions, and several statements were made while promoting and defending The Idol against reporting about its set. Professional norm and promotional duty explain much of it.

claims.claim: She expected to improvise Nosferatu's movement ("I thought I was just going to go and freak out and we'll improvise. And then I got there and it was very much choreographed") and told Portman, "I was grateful not to have to shape it on my own" (Interview, December 2024). To Vanity Fair: "I didn't realize how choreographed it was going to be, but that helped infuse every moment with an intention."
claims.passage: Before _Nosferatu_ she expected to improvise the possession scenes, and they turned out to be tightly choreographed. "I was grateful not to have to shape it on my own,"
claims.inference: Uncertainty about whether she is "doing it right" is resolved by the director and by structure, which she experiences as comfort rather than constraint.
claims.alternative: Eggers is famously exacting and any actor on his set would credit the framework. In the same junket she insists the inner work is her own: "At the end of the day, there's always work that has to be done within yourself, and that's very personal" (AU Review, 2024).

claims.claim: On March 2, 2023, the day after Rolling Stone's report on The Idol, Entertainment Tonight published her statement calling Sam Levinson "the best director I have ever worked with" and saying "Never have I felt more supported or respected in a creative space, my input and opinions more valued."
claims.passage: "Sam is, for so many reasons, the best director I have ever worked with. Never have I felt more supported or respected in a creative space, my input and opinions more valued."
claims.inference: A public defense of an embattled collaborator, given in personal terms; the 2016 post (C73), Cannes remark (C67), 2024 interview (C69, C70) and podcast (C71) continue the record.
claims.alternative: As the lead whose scenes the reporting concerned, defending the show also defended her own experience and judgment, which is how she framed it (C68). Promotional duty applies. No source shows a cost to her.

claims.claim: Rolling Stone's May 23, 2023 follow-up summarized its March 1 report: interviews with 13 cast and crew members produced claims that on-set conditions were "often chaotic," and crew members said the show's direction changed after original director Amy Seimetz left and Levinson stepped in.
claims.passage: said 13 cast and crew members had described an "often chaotic" set and a show that changed after its original director, Amy Seimetz, left and Levinson stepped in.
claims.inference: Context for her defense; the claims concern her own role. Attribute every allegation and do not adjudicate it.

claims.claim: She made no public comment during her father's 2022 defamation trial against Amber Heard (Fairfax County, Virginia, April 11 to June 1, 2022), which frustrated some of his fans, per Jezebel. She explained the choice to Elle in November 2022 (C75, C76).
claims.passage: against Heard, she said nothing in public, which frustrated some of his fans,
claims.inference: As an adult she chose privacy and self-definition over public comment, in contrast with her public defense at 17.
claims.alternative: Her own stated reasons are privacy and self-definition; she was also raised to protect privacy (C21). Legal caution is possible but unstated. A Four reading would stress the self-definition; a Six reading would stress caution in a public minefield. Jezebel misstates her 2016 age as 15 (CBS/AP: 17); Jezebel's "speaks volumes" is the writer's opinion.

claims.claim: She frames privacy as protection against an intrusive public: "I'm not here to give myself to the world to be eaten alive" (Elle, 2022), said after "people feel like they know you, even though they don't."
claims.passage: Her line on fame itself is blunter: "I'm not here to give myself to the world to be eaten alive."
claims.inference: Privacy is a family norm and a craft rationale (anonymity helps audiences believe her characters). Her stated reasons are protective against an intrusive public.
claims.alternative: Elle's writer reads it as "a similar craving for mystique" (Four-compatible). Upbringing alone explains much of it.

claims.claim: To Portman (October 2024), directly after "This industry can be so crazy and you can lose your footing really easily": "I feel like it's corny because people always say this, but you have to have people around you that you've known forever that are going to anchor you."
claims.passage: "I feel like it's corny because people always say this, but you have to have people around you that you've known forever that are going to anchor you."
claims.inference: Repeatedly, danger or loss of control is met by holding on to trusted people and routines; this is the security strategy the Six reading predicts.
claims.alternative: Valuing close people is common and also fits Types 2 and 9. Harper's Bazaar UK's "Loyalty... ranks highly for Depp" is the writer's framing; her words are "I love people who love their people."

claims.claim: Asked about sensing people wanting her to fail, she said, "Yeah, but it just is what it is" (Vanity Fair, 2024). She also self-deflates ("Girl, you don't matter that much," i-D, 2023) and self-soothes ("Everything is mental. I'm good. I'm chilling," Interview, 2024).
claims.passage: Of people wanting her to fail: "it just is what it is."
claims.inference: Self-soothing and self-deflation in the face of worry; this cuts against a Four's sense of being special or exempt.
claims.alternative: Minimizing and "it is what it is" also fit Type 9; self-deprecation is a common defense for a famous child under scrutiny.

claims.claim: She told Vanity Fair (November 2024), "I feel like people have been ready to see me fail, in a way, since I was a kid. That has made me only want to work harder and prove people wrong."
claims.passage: "I feel like people have been ready to see me fail, in a way, since I was a kid. That has made me only want to work harder and prove people wrong."
claims.inference: Effort and preparation are her response to suspicion and self-doubt.
claims.alternative: Wanting to be seen as a hard worker fits Type 3 image concerns as well as the Six's preparation. Testimony is from her mother and a promoting co-star.

claims.claim: In her November 2022 Elle interview, asked about the "nepo baby" debate, she said "nothing is going to get you the part except for being right for the part" and, later in the answer, "Maybe you get your foot in the door, but you still just have your foot in the door." The remarks drew a backlash (PAPER).
claims.passage: She said "nothing is going to get you the part except for being right for the part." Later in the answer: "Maybe you get your foot in the door, but you still just have your foot in the door."
claims.inference: She adjusted her public framing after criticism; her acknowledgment of an unusual childhood predates the backlash.
claims.alternative: The adjustment fits a Six's sensitivity to the group and a Three's image management equally; it does not discriminate.

claims.claim: She told Harper's Bazaar UK (January 2025) that Edward Scissorhands upset her at three, "Not because I thought he was scary, but because everyone was being so mean to him and I got really upset."
claims.passage: At three, Edward Scissorhands upset her "because everyone was being so mean to him," she told Harper's Bazaar UK.
claims.inference: The strongest Type 4 material: empathy for the mistreated outsider and an aesthetic pull toward dark, complicated feeling.
claims.alternative: She was promoting a gothic horror film; genre and profession supply much of this. She qualifies it in the same breath: "I laugh a lot in my own life. I'm a happy person, so I like to explore the underbelly of that at work." The "am I sick" line is a half-joking aside.

claims.claim: She calls acting "an emotional outlet for me—I feel like it helps me, I don't know, heal things with myself, perhaps" (Vanity Fair, 2024), and in 2019 said it may be "the only place where I can really let myself go."
claims.passage: "It's an emotional outlet for me—I feel like it helps me, I don't know, heal things with myself, perhaps," she told Vanity Fair.
claims.inference: Expression of deep personal feeling through art fits the Four's search for self-expression.
claims.alternative: She generalizes it herself ("a lot of us do this for that reason"); drawing on real emotion is the standard account of naturalistic acting.

claims.claim: Asked by Knightley (2021) whether she worried about being judged because of her parents: "I'm not the same kind of actor as my dad or my mom, and I'm very much my own person... that doesn't mean you can't become your own artist, or that your own art isn't valuable on its own." Further inward answers: C92 (2025), C93 (2026), C100 (2024), C12 (2024).
claims.passage: "I'm not the same kind of actor as my dad or my mom, and I'm very much my own person."
claims.inference: Strong counterevidence to an outward-only reading: she often anchors in her own distinctness, reasons and path. She also describes this as learned over time ("I've had to grow into that feeling"; "Désormais" = now, as opposed to before).
claims.alternative: Identity talk arises specifically from being the child of two famous artists, which any type in her position would face. Whether "know in my heart" reads as a Four's felt authenticity or a Six's conviction is a judgment call.

claims.claim: She describes herself as "full of dualities" (Portman, 2024: "I feel like I've always been full of dualities, and my double culture adds to that"), and as having "so many sides" (Harper's Bazaar UK, 2025).
claims.passage: She calls herself "full of dualities."
claims.inference: Four-compatible self-image of paradox.
claims.alternative: Her own explanation is literal: a bicultural, bilingual upbringing and a shy child who became "quite performative." In 2021 she said "I don't know if I feel like I have different personalities."

claims.claim: She told Elle (2022), "I'm not interested in making anything that doesn't challenge me, or challenge other people, honestly."
claims.passage: she told Elle she wants work that will "challenge me, or challenge other people."
claims.inference: A provocation-tolerant taste that argues against a conflict-avoidant Nine and fits a Four's distinctness; it also sits awkwardly with a cautious Six (see C103).
claims.alternative: Artistic ambition common among young actors seeking auteur work; also fits an appetite for challenge.

claims.claim: She told Vanity Fair (2024) she does not do method acting because "I'm too attached to my life," then, in the next paragraph of the interview, "This movie had such an immersive energy about it that I do think I brought the darkness home, for sure... I was carrying her with me when I was at home."
claims.passage: She avoids method acting because "I'm too attached to my life," but after _Nosferatu_, "I do think I brought the darkness home, for sure."
claims.inference: The boundary between work and life is porous; this undercuts any claim that she keeps darkness strictly contained at work.
claims.alternative: Four-compatible depth of identification; also a common account of an immersive shoot. She keeps a line back to ordinary life (calls home, "chat jovially").

claims.claim: Robert Eggers told Deadline, as quoted by Hello! (December 2024), "Myself, the casting director, and even the videographer were in tears, because it was so powerful."
claims.passage: "Myself, the casting director, and even the videographer were in tears, because it was so powerful."
claims.inference: Independent confirmation, from the director, of the audition's effect; testimony to commitment, not to motive.
claims.alternative: Promotional testimony from her director, reported second-hand; the original Deadline interview was not opened. A studio featurette (S39) has Eggers say the same in different words.

claims.claim: On the January 2025 Happy Sad Confused podcast, asked whether she felt her parentage as a shadow, she said, "I'm not ashamed, like, my parents are such talented performers."
claims.passage: Asked on the podcast about her parents' shadow, she said, "I'm not ashamed."
claims.inference: Comparison is present but described as admiration and closeness.
claims.alternative: Elsewhere she compares herself with her mother, framed as admiration ("You're so much prettier than me," said "half-joking," i-D 2023; "En vrai, on est très semblables," ELLE France via Purepeople 2026). A Four reading would treat comparison as envy; the record does not support that intensity.

claims.claim: Interpretation: counting her own words in the opened sources, fear and anxiety about her own life appear in six first-person sources spread across 2021-2025 (S03, S05, S02, S07, S01, S09). Shame-family words about herself are rare and light: a joke that looking like a corpse was "a workout for my self-esteem," the half-joking "am I sick for feeling that way?", and "I'm about to super embarrass myself in front of Robert Eggers" about the accent. On the 2025 podcast she says outright, "I'm not ashamed." Shame language in her answers is mostly about Ellen ("a girl who's just super ashamed of this pull").
claims.passage: Fear comes up about her own life in six of her interviews from 2021 to 2025: work, fame, strangers, physical risk and politics.
claims.inference: On the 9takes triad framing (fear triad 5/6/7, shame triad 2/3/4), the hard emotion in her self-report is fear, which she names and uses rather than pushes down (7) or detaches from (5).
claims.alternative: The count is crude and confounded: two of the six sources promote a horror film, Knightley asked about anxiety directly, and nerves are standard junket material. Her worry about strangers thinking she is "weird or rude" has a shame flavor.

claims.claim: Interpretation: what she protects, and how. Her stated reasons for privacy, normal life and holding on to her people are threat-based ("eaten alive," "lose your footing," "things get dangerous," "feel powerless," "not go insane"), and her steadying moves point to trusted people, directors and structures (C10, C11, C16, C17, C22). That pattern runs from 2021 to 2025 and across work, fame, family privacy and politics. It is the case for Type 6.
claims.passage: She talks about her fear often, steadies it with people and structures she trusts, and inside that safety she takes big creative risks.
claims.inference: Leading reading: a security motive that seeks safety in trusted people and frameworks and keeps fear active as fuel.
claims.alternative: She also anchors in her own reasons and path (C12, C28), increasingly so by 2024-2026; she frames the 2023 Idol defense through her own experience; profession and promotional duty explain much of the trust talk.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the strongest alternative is Type 4. Her pull toward darkness and the mistreated outsider (C26), acting as the one place she can "let myself go" and draw on deeply personal feeling (C27), her many-sidedness (C29), her taste for the strange (C30), her search for "my own identity" and conviction "in my heart" (C28), and the porous line between role and life (C32) all fit the Four. What weakens it: the Four material is concentrated in how she talks about art, roles and taste; her identity statements arise from being a famous couple's child; she deflates her own specialness ("Girl, you don't matter that much"); she calls herself "a happy person" and prizes ordinary routine; and her privacy is defended against danger rather than against being misunderstood.
claims.passage: That overlap is why this read is medium confidence and not high.
claims.inference: Four explains her aesthetic and creative life better than the Six does; Six explains her relational and security choices better. The inward-resolution statements (C12, C28, C92, C93, C100) fit both, which caps confidence at medium.
claims.alternative: If the work talk is taken as the truest window on her inner life, the Four reading gains; an actor's junket answers may also understate melancholy she keeps private.

claims.claim: On the January 2025 podcast she said she is usually relaxed about auditions because "my mom always said to me, like, you know, roles go to the people who are meant to play them. And I totally believe that in my heart." The article uses this as the strongest Type 9 signal and answers it with her frequent naming of fear and her wish to "challenge other people" (C30).
claims.passage: She is usually relaxed about auditions, she said on the podcast, because her mother taught her that "roles go to the people who are meant to play them."
claims.inference: Nine is the most serious secondary alternative after Four.
claims.alternative: Mixed signals are expected from a 27-year-old whose record is almost entirely promotional interviews.

claims.claim: As of October 16, 2026, the opened record contains no long-form testimony from family or close friends about her private conduct; outside testimony is limited to her mother's brief 2023 defense, her security guard's "like a daughter," and promotional praise from collaborators. Nearly all first-person evidence comes from cover stories, junkets and awards campaigns.
claims.passage: As of October 2026 there is no long-form testimony from the people closest to her, only her mother's defense, her longtime security guard's remark that she is "like a daughter" to him, and praise from collaborators in release weeks.
claims.inference: The record cannot show how she behaves when a trusted relationship fails, which would be the best test of a Six's loyalty and a Four's identity motive.
claims.alternative: Absence of testimony reflects her privacy norm, not necessarily anything about type.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if a memoir, long profile with named intimates, or a collaborator's detailed account is published.

claims.claim: 9takes types her father, Johnny Depp, as an Enneagram Type 4 on its live personality-analysis page (checked October 16, 2026).
claims.passage: It would be easy to say the Four runs in the family, since 9takes reads her father,
claims.inference: Relevant only for internal links; a parent's typing is not evidence about her.
claims.alternative: Inheriting a parent's type is a temptation to resist, not an argument.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if the Johnny Depp page is retyped.

claims.claim: She auditioned for Nosferatu over Zoom from her family's place in the French countryside; one scene was "a big freak-out scene," and she told Vanity Fair (November 2024) she gathered things to throw: "I had a roll of paper towels, and some books, and I just threw shit all over the room. I started moving around like crazy. I wanted to show that I wasn't scared to go there."
claims.passage: "I had a roll of paper towels, and some books, and I just threw shit all over the room. I started moving around like crazy. I wanted to show that I wasn't scared to go there."
claims.inference: The opening scene: named nerves, then full commitment; she frames the goal as showing she was not scared.
claims.alternative: Her own account in an awards-campaign interview; the role required this extremity ("I felt like my job was to show him that I could go there"), so it shows commitment to a brief, not going beyond it.

claims.claim: Interpretation (author's count, see C36): fear is the hard feeling she names about herself most often in the opened interviews from 2021 to 2025.
claims.passage: By my count of her interviews from 2021 to 2025, fear is the hard feeling she names about herself most often.
claims.inference: Sets up the triad argument; labeled in the prose as the author's count.
claims.alternative: Crude and confounded count (junket context, a direct anxiety question, a horror-film press cycle), stated with its limits in the first "Why not Type 4?" reason.

claims.claim: Interpretation: across work and life she walks toward frightening work inside a trusted frame (directors, co-stars, long-held friends) and steps back from risk outside one (no skydiving, no Twitter, retreat into normal life).
claims.passage: Inside a frame she trusts (a director with a plan, a trusted co-star, friends she has known forever), she walks toward what scares her.
claims.inference: The article's central mechanism, reconciling her named fear with her bold roles without using a counterphobic label; it predicts that big risks without a trusted frame would weaken the Six reading (C62).
claims.alternative: Leaving school at 16 on gut instinct (C02) and her taste for provocation (C103) are partial counterexamples, named in "What the type doesn't explain." Profession and promotional duty explain some of the trust language (C51).

claims.claim: In the same i-D answer (February 2023) she quoted her self-talk: "Okay, I really don't want to fuck this up, so let me work as hard as I possibly can to make sure that I have left no rock unturned."
claims.passage: The answer goes on, and she quotes her own self-talk: "Okay, I really don't want to fuck this up, so let me work as hard as I possibly can to make sure that I have left no rock unturned."
claims.inference: Exhaustive preparation as the response to doubt; the worry is about failing the job.
claims.alternative: Converting nerves to effort also fits Types 3 and 1.

claims.claim: Interpretation: faith in the people who chose her, exhaustive preparation and fear kept as fuel, in one i-D answer, together match the Six's strategies.
claims.passage: That is a Six's toolkit, laid out in one answer.
claims.inference: Author's reading of C11, C46 and C14 together.
claims.alternative: A single answer, framed in part by the writer; each element alone fits other types.

claims.claim: Asked by Keira Knightley (Interview, 2021) whether she suffers from anxiety on set, she said "Definitely," that it peaks right before she starts something, and that she can get in her head: "Am I going to be able to do this? What have I signed up for? Are they sure that I'm the one?"
claims.passage: "Definitely," she said. Before a job starts she can get in her head: "Am I going to be able to do this? What have I signed up for? Are they sure that I'm the one?"
claims.inference: Anticipatory doubt about capability and about whether the choosers were right.
claims.alternative: A direct question from a co-star invites a confession of nerves.

claims.claim: On the Happy Sad Confused podcast (January 2025) she said of Eggers, "I had that trust with him because I knew that no matter where he was leading me it was going to be a great place to be."
claims.passage: "I had that trust with him because I knew that no matter where he was leading me it was going to be a great place to be."
claims.inference: Trust in a director as the condition for letting go.
claims.alternative: Any actor on an Eggers set credits his framework; promotional context. Podcast transcription by two models, one sentence.

claims.claim: On the podcast she said Eggers is "not going to let you leave until that scene is perfect" and added that there is "comfort in that."
claims.passage: Eggers, she said on the podcast, is "not going to let you leave until that scene is perfect," and she found "comfort in that."
claims.inference: Structure experienced as comfort rather than constraint.
claims.alternative: The transcript has a spoken repetition ("there's there's comfort in that"); the article quotes only the shared words. In the same junket she insists the inner work is her own (AU Review, S15).

claims.claim: She also frames demanding roles as appetite: "I really like emotional scenes because they're challenging. I feel stimulated by that" (Vanity Fair, 2024).
claims.passage: "I really like emotional scenes because they're challenging. I feel stimulated by that," she told Vanity Fair.
claims.inference: Counterweight to a fear-only reading of her role choices; the article says trust language alone proves little.
claims.alternative: Also "There's nothing more fun to me than sinking my teeth into something" (Elle, 2022). Trust-and-safety language is standard on sexually explicit productions.

claims.claim: Asked by Portman whether she would go to space, she said, "No, I am so scared. [Laughs]"
claims.passage: When Portman asked whether she would go to space, Depp laughed: "No, I am so scared."
claims.inference: Light, laughing context for the "scared of everything" line.
claims.alternative: Banter, not a statement of a lasting state.

claims.claim: Asked what happened, she told Portman, "I think the world started to scare me a lot. I'm super scared of things that I used to not be scared of," and after Portman's "Dang," "I wonder if I'm more aware of the dangers of the world or something?"
claims.passage: "I think the world started to scare me a lot," she said, and a moment later: "I wonder if I'm more aware of the dangers of the world or something?"
claims.inference: Anticipatory vigilance about danger, in her own explanation.
claims.alternative: Same light exchange about thrill activities.

claims.claim: She told i-D (2023) that fame can make her paranoid and that she overthinks being photographed: "If I leave my house and I look like shit and someone takes a photo, is it going to be, 'She looks like hell, she must be depressed?'"
claims.passage: She told i-D she overthinks being photographed: "If I leave my house and I look like shit and someone takes a photo, is it going to be, 'She looks like hell, she must be depressed?'"
claims.inference: Worst-case scanning about public exposure.
claims.alternative: Fame supplies real intrusions; the worry is also about being judged (shame-compatible). She says she handles it by self-deflation.

claims.claim: Elle (2022) reported that when strangers approach her she fears not for her safety but "that they're going to think I'm really weird or rude because I just get really shy and kind of anxious."
claims.passage: she worries "that they're going to think I'm really weird or rude because I just get really shy and kind of anxious."
claims.inference: Social anxiety in public.
claims.alternative: The worry is about being judged, which the article labels shame territory and counts against the clean fear reading.

claims.claim: She told Portman (2024), "This industry can be so crazy and you can lose your footing really easily."
claims.passage: "This industry can be so crazy and you can lose your footing really easily," she told Portman.
claims.inference: Threat framing of fame.
claims.alternative: A common observation about show business.

claims.claim: After the November 2024 US election she told Harper's Bazaar UK, "I feel we're going backwards, which is endlessly disheartening and heartbreaking... It's a horrific time, and I'm scared, and I'm sad."
claims.passage: "It's a horrific time, and I'm scared, and I'm sad."
claims.inference: Fear named about politics, outside a promotional answer about her work.
claims.alternative: Election fear was widespread among her peers.

claims.claim: Right after the election remarks, Harper's Bazaar UK quoted her: "When things feel out of control and you feel powerless, you have to hold tight to the people you love and look after those people."
claims.passage: "When things feel out of control and you feel powerless, you have to hold tight to the people you love and look after those people."
claims.inference: Her own link between fear/powerlessness and allegiance; the most Six-specific line in the record.
claims.alternative: The magazine frames it as prioritising "loyalty and friendship"; valuing close people also fits Types 2 and 9.

claims.claim: Interpretation: C58 is the clearest first-person link between fear and allegiance in the record and was not said about her own work.
claims.passage: That is the clearest link in her record between fear and allegiance, and it was about politics, not a film she was selling.
claims.inference: Author's weighting of C58.
claims.alternative: It was still said during a Nosferatu press interview.

claims.claim: She told Vanity Fair (2024), "I'm not an internet rat like that. I'm not on Twitter. I'm not reading stuff," and "I try to protect myself from all that."
claims.passage: She told Vanity Fair, "I'm not on Twitter. I'm not reading stuff."
claims.inference: Stepping back from exposure outside a trusted frame.
claims.alternative: Common advice for public figures.

claims.claim: She told Elle (2022), "That's why I like to do my work and put as much of my heart into it as I can and then retreat back into my real life and just be a normal person."
claims.passage: She told Elle she likes to "retreat back into my real life and just be a normal person."
claims.inference: Retreat into ordinary life as protection.
claims.alternative: Also a family norm (C77).

claims.claim: Interpretation: the frame mechanism (C44) is falsifiable; big risks without trusted people or structure would weaken it.
claims.passage: That claim can be tested. If she started taking big risks with no trusted people or structure around her, the Six reading would weaken.
claims.inference: States what would count against the reading.
claims.alternative: C02 is a partial past counterexample.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check when new long-form interviews or testimony describe her taking a major risk alone, or describe how she acted when a trusted frame failed.

claims.passage: She won't jump out of a plane.

claims.inference: The denials that sit beside the allegations.

claims.passage: Rolling Stone noted that its report had included statements from Depp defending the series.

claims.passage: At Cannes that May she said, "it's always sad and disheartening to hear mean, false things about someone you care about, and it wasn't my experience shooting the show."

claims.passage: In November 2024, with the series panned and cancelled, she told Vanity Fair, "But I stand by it. We made a choice and we went for it."

claims.inference: Dated context for the 2022 silence; a minor-era public act, not used as type evidence.

And I'm really ready to be defined for the things that I put out there."
claims.passage: She went on that people have "really wanted to define me by the men in my life," and that she was "really ready to be defined for the things that I put out there."
claims.inference: Self-definition as a second stated reason (Four-compatible).

claims.passage: "I've just been raised in a manner that has taught me that privacy is something that's important to protect," she told Elle.

claims.alternative: Elle's writer reads it as "a similar craving for mystique."

claims.passage: So she vouched publicly for her father in 2016, stayed silent about him in 2022, and vouched publicly for her director in 2023.

claims.passage: Three months later she told i-D, "I'm so careful about these conversations now."
claims.inference: An adjustment after criticism.

claims.claim: Asked by Vanity Fair (November 2024) whether she had struggled with insecurity, she said "Absolutely" and quoted herself calling the hardest part of the role "Getting over the imposter syndrome of, like, 'Why am I here and why do these people think that I can do this?'"
claims.passage: "Absolutely," she said, and called the hardest part of _Nosferatu_ "getting over the imposter syndrome of, like, 'Why am I here and why do these people think that I can do this?'"
claims.inference: Doubt about belonging and about the judgment of the people who chose her.

claims.inference: The article counts this shift toward the Four reading.

claims.claim: She told Vanity Fair (2024) the feeling that people want her to fail is "Not in a vindictive way at all, but just in a sense of, like, fuel to my fire," and "I do want to prove that I'm a hard worker and I'm not here for anything else but to work hard."
claims.passage: She called it "fuel to my fire," and said, "I do want to prove that I'm a hard worker and I'm not here for anything else but to work hard."

type_hypothesis.against: (1) She often resolves doubt inward. 2021: "I'm very much my own person" and nerves are "a sign that I'm invested" (C10, C28). 2024: the hoped-for answer to imposter syndrome is to feel "confident enough within myself," and "If people still want to talk shit... that's not my problem" (C12, C28). 2025: "I just need to know in my heart why I'm doing something" and "be steadfast in your conviction" (C28). 2026: pleasing everyone "ce n'est pas mon ambition... il faut tracer sa route" (C28). (2) Strong Type 4 material: empathy for the mistreated outsider and a pull to "the darker underbelly of things" (C26); acting as the one place she can "really let myself go" and "heal things with myself" (C27); "full of dualities" and "so many sides" (C29); "weird and wonderful," "challenge other people" (C30); the darkness she "brought... home" from Nosferatu (C32). (3) She is often calm, not anxious, about outcomes: usually relaxed at auditions because "roles go to the people who are meant to play them," "Everything happens for a reason," "it just is what it is" (C13, C23, C39), which also points to Type 9. (4) Type 3 signals: "prove people wrong," "I do want to prove that I'm a hard worker," a decade as a Chanel face, and "Humility is incredibly important, especially in this business" as a stated professional norm (C04, C12, C24, C25). (5) Circumstance explains much of the Six evidence: trust-and-safety talk is industry-standard on sexually explicit productions and much of it was said while promoting and defending The Idol (C16, C18); two key sources are horror-film junkets that inflate fear vocabulary (C36); privacy was taught by famous parents (C21); her Idol defense is framed through her own experience as the lead, and no source shows it cost her anything (C18). (6) As an adult she stayed silent about her father during the 2022 trial and explained it as privacy and self-definition, which does not fit a simple loyalty reading (C20). (7) Early self-direction: leaving school at 16 on "really strong gut instincts" (C02). (8) The record shows no skeptical or authority-testing side, which many Sixes display; it shows trust in authorities, not testing of them.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4 explains her aesthetic and creative life well. She identifies with the mistreated outsider (Edward Scissorhands, "a little bit of empathy for Nosferatu"), is "interested in the darker underbelly of things," and says she is "better at crying than laughing" (C26). Acting is "the only place where I can really let myself go," an "emotional outlet" that may "heal things with myself," drawn from a place that is "deeply personal" (C27). She calls herself "full of dualities" and "a Gemini" with "a lot of sides" (C29), seeks "weird and wonderful" work and "the weird stuff" (C30), merges with roles to "an utter, complete togetherness with the character" (C32), and resolves doubt by being "very much my own person," finding "my own identity," and knowing "in my heart" why she does things (C28). On this reading her nerves are ordinary performance anxiety and her trust talk is professional courtesy. What strains Type 4: the Four material is concentrated in talk about art, roles and taste, and her identity statements arise specifically from being two famous artists' child. She deflates her own specialness ("Girl, you don't matter that much," C23), calls herself "a happy person" (C26) who prizes the butcher, the grocery store and simple stew (C22), says "I'm not ashamed" of her parentage (C35), and expresses comparison with her mother as admiration rather than envy (C35). Her reasons for privacy are about danger ("eaten alive," "things get dangerous") rather than being misunderstood (C21, C22), and the hard emotion she names about herself is fear, not shame or longing (C36).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What her steadying moves protect against, and which hard emotion she names about herself. On the 9takes triad map the Four uses shame (identity, deficiency, longing) and the Six uses fear (security, support, preparation). A Four guards a distinct inner self from being misread and dwells on what is missing in her; a Six guards against danger by anchoring in trusted people, authorities and structures and keeps fear active as fuel. Her record leans Six on three specific, repeated observations. First, fear about her own life appears in six first-person sources across 2021-2025, in work, fame, strangers, physical risk and politics (C15, C36), and she says she keeps and uses it ("I like the fear a little bit," "fuel to my fire," C14). Shame about herself is rare and joking, and she says "I'm not ashamed" (C35, C36). Second, her stated reasons for privacy and ordinary life are threat-based ("eaten alive," "lose your footing," "things get dangerous," "not go insane"), and when things feel "out of control" her answer is "hold tight to the people you love" (C21, C22). Third, uncertainty about her work is resolved by trusted directors and frameworks: "you never know if you're doing it right... until... conversations with the director," "grateful not to have to shape it on my own," "no matter where he was leading me it was going to be a great place to be" (C16, C17). The inward statements (C12, C28) are real and grow more frequent from 2024 to 2026, but she frames them as effortful and learned ("I definitely have struggled with that," "I've had to grow into that feeling," "Désormais"). That is consistent with a Six reaching for inner authority, but it is also what a Four who has outgrown a famous family would say. This discriminator is partial, not decisive: it rests on promotional interviews, and two of the six fear sources promote a horror film. The cleanest available test is the Werwulf press cycle (December 2026 to January 2027): asked what steadied her through a grounded, physically transformed role, does she credit trusted people, Eggers's structure and preparation (6), or her own distinct feeling and identity (4)? Drafting note (2026-10-16): the article states the pattern as a mechanism, not a counterphobic label: inside a trusted frame she walks toward what scares her, outside one she steps back (C44). It names what would count against it (C62) and the past counterexample of leaving school at 16 (C02).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her early, decisive self-direction (leaving school at 16 on gut instinct) and sustained appetite for provocation ("challenge other people"; on the podcast, The Idol was "pushing like society's buttons, I think intentionally") sit awkwardly with a cautious Six. Her 2022 silence about her father, against her public loyalty to Levinson in 2023, has no stated explanation beyond privacy and self-definition. The record shows no skeptical or authority-testing behavior. The more inward tone of 2024-2026 could reflect growth, or could mean the Six reading overweights junket nerves. There is no intimate testimony showing how she acts when a trusted relationship fails (C40). Minor-era disclosures in the public record (a 2016 ELLE France account of past anorexia, reported by La Libre; a 2015 Self-Evident Truths photo and her 2016 clarification) are deliberately excluded from the type argument; using either causally would invent a wound. Wing and instinctual variant are not established; a 6w7 or 6w5 reading would be speculation.
